utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Whom should I address? Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will be responsible for leading the next witness, Mr. Rajko Gusa. No protective measures and the witness is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Since we have time available, what is the best way to pronounce your name? Is it the English or the French way?

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: It is Du-Toit, Your Honour, and it is in French, it is Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can already proceed. I see no objections against admission of the 92 ter statement; is that true? Of course, if the attestations are received and we have no attachments to them, there's just a map which --

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: There's just a map that I would like to add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... would like to introduce, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: -- to the 65 ter list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to have it added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... because I disclosed it to the Defence, and it's 65 ter 5490. So I would request to add it to the 65 ter list, and ... [Overlapping Speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no objection against adding it to the 65 ter list. That is already on the record. Do you want to make it an attachment or would you like to introduce it separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: I would like to introduce it maybe at the end of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Gusa, good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please stand. Yes. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text of that solemn declaration is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please read the words aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusa. Please be seated. Mr. Gusa, you'll first be examined by Mr. Du-Toit, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gusa. Can you please state your full names for the record.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Rajko Gusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Is it correct that you made two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I please call up 65 ter 5431.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, right in front of you is the first statement that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of May and 28th of May, 1997. It's in front of you with your signature. Can you just confirm that is your statement, please?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we just move to page 2 of this statement, please. Mr. President, I just want to place on the record, as you can see on page two of the statement, there is paragraph numbers inserted in hand to the left-hand side of the statement. That was not part of the original statement, but when the witness was seen again in 2008, that was added just to make it easier to refer back to specific paragraphs of the statements. So that's why you see that these paragraph numbers are inserted in hand. I just want it place that on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They are added afterwards. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, can I then -- can you please call up 65 ter 5432, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, is it correct that this is the second statement that was taken by members of this office on the 19th of February, 2008. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I just move also to page 2 of that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 3 of the statement, Mr. Gusa, sort of round about in the middle, just one point of clarification there, and I quote: "There were about ten houses in my neighbourhood that I could see, and they were all hit by the shells. All of the houses were subsequently burnt and looted." Now, this incident, this that you saw, did you see that on the 4th of August or was it later?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: This was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Gusa, is it correct that when you arrived in The Hague, you were again given the opportunity to read through the B/C/S versions of both of these statements?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And do these statements accurately reflect the information that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And is the information contained in these two statements true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And if you were asked in court today the same questions, would your answers be the same as you have given twice to members of our office?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I think I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move the two statements into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 05431 becomes Exhibit number P959; and 65 ter 05432 becomes Exhibit number P960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P959, being the 1997 statement, and P960, the February 2008 statement, are admitted into evidence. Mr. Du-Toit, one question about the paragraph 3 you just mentioned. You were talking about an incident and you started reading: "There were about ten houses in my neighbourhood that I could see, and they were hit by shells." Witness, did you observe yourself that they were hit by shell the or did you afterwards later see the houses damaged by shells that had hit them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only saw the first one, mine. The other ones I saw later on. In October, I was taken to the village. One of their inspectors took me two days in a row, and then I saw that everything had been burnt down and destroyed. There were some ten or so houses that were left standing. Everything else had been looted and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You confused me a bit when you asked about observing the incident, rather than observing the consequences of apparent shelling. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I am supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit, will now read a summary of your statement, so that the public knows what your testimony is about. Please proceed, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witness was living in the village of Zemunik Gornji, municipality of Zadar, at the time of Operation Storm. From 10.00 in the morning on the 4th of August, 1995, his village was heavily shelled by the Croatian army, and his house was hit by a number of shells. After the shelling stopped at around 2200 hours, the witness fled to the village of Bukovic. Around 300 Croatian soldiers entered Bukovic and immediately five or six houses were set ablaze. The witness fled Bukovic and hid in the forest on the mountain of Zmistak. From his vantage point, the witness was able to view the villages of Kistanje and Ervenik. He saw the whole village of Kistanje on fire at a time when there was heavy military traffic moving through the village. The smaller villages of Biovicino Selo and Kolasac were also burnt. He also witnessed burning of houses in the village of Ervenik and looting by Croatian soldiers from the homes and farms in the area. Trucks loaded with looted property and stolen livestock were driven away by soldiers on the main road with the loads only displayed. In early 1995, the witness surrendered to a Croatian policeman who was a friend of a Serb family in Ervenik. He was taken to Knin and then further to Zadar. In the detention facility in Zadar, he was beaten. He was held in Zadar for three to four months, and then taken to Split prison when he was detained until October 1996. That is the end of the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I can just call up 65 ter 5490. That is the orientation map of this witness. Mr. President, as you can see, this was just prepared by members of our office to just orient the different places referred to by the witness in -- especially in his first statement that is already admitted. And as you can see, the numbers from 1 to 9 depicts certain key places that the witness mentioned in his evidence. And as you can see, to the left hand of the map, there is also a legend, indicating the different place names and also references to some aspects of the paragraphs of the 28th of May 1997 statement. And I would also like to move this map into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently, no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P961 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is all that I have for the witness at the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who will be the first to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour. One moment please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, in a second, Mr. Misetic, who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina, will cross-examine you, and he is seated to your left -- or he is standing to your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It will just take one minute, Your Honour, to release the documents to the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gusa.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The first point I'd like to take you to is your military service in the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. You, in fact, were a soldier from 1991 up until Operation Storm. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, can you describe for the Court what, if any, role you had in the defence of the so-called Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: In the beginning, I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I didn't want to go, and then I was imprisoned in Knin; and then later I was released and I was in the Territorial Defence in my village throughout this period up until Operation Storm. I was never on the lines, and also the lines between our army and the Croatian army was about 100 metres away --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 800 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, your village is on the front line, isn't it, sir? Sorry. It was on the front line?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, if you were standing guard in your village and your village is on the front line, then you were a guard on the front lines. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No. I was not on the front line, I was in the background. It is a different thing to on the front line, and it is quite different to be in the rear. I was in the village, where the houses were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, the command -- there was command post in your village, correct? Isn't that what you were guarding?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what was the command post of?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: It was the command post --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask him again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was the command post of? The interpreters didn't hear you, if you could repeat that again, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Oh, it was a military command post, the Serbian army command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you seem to be making a distinction in your statement between you being a member of the Territorial Defence and not being a member of the army. Can you explain what you believe to be the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: The difference is in this. The real soldiers were on the front line and the Territorial Defence were for the people who weren't really capable to participate in real war, in warfare; for instance, one-on-one, so on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have 1D47-0030, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, I'd ask you to take a look at this document. It is from the 180th Motor Brigade. It is dated 13 March 1992. It's from the military police to the 180th Motor Brigade, and it discusses security duty was conducted in the barracks and that there were searches conducted. And if you look under part 2, your name appears, Gusa, P. Rajko, with a VP number. Were you, in fact, a member of the 180th Motor Brigade in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I ask that this exhibit be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D823, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D823 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page of this document, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you look at number 9 there, Mr. Gusa, is that you, date of birth 25 August, 1956, born in Gornji Zemunik?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were you, in fact, conscripted into the 180 Motor Brigade on the 3rd of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Nor do I know what brigade this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now have 1D47-0034, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. We'll wait for the English to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is again a military police document. And at number 2, it reports a reassignment of the following conscripts on the 1st of March, 1992; and at number 2, it says, "Gusa, Petar Rajko." Do you recall being reassigned from one --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. I was reassigned, and I was then reassigned to the village of Kosare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the bottom of the document, it says: "Military conscripts to be issued weapons, ammunition, and mine explosive devices, and sent to barracks NHS Macura, Benkovac." Do you recall been send to a barracks in Benkovac, on or around the 1st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall on or about the 1st of March being taken over by senior officer from the 1st Motor Brigade and transported to the unit by bus?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D824.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D824 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, on the 1st of March, apparently, the witness is reassigned from 4810-84 to 4810-7. On the 13th of March, however, such request in relation to apparently the witness locates him at 4810-10. Is that mystery or that puzzle further to be explored?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Partly a mystery, but I will get into some more details of his background in a few minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may have 1D47-0037 on the screen, please. Your Honour, we were not able to upload this into e-court in time last night, so we have a hard copy for the witness and we will show it via Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, this is a document dated 1 June 1992, and it reports to with a disciplinary measure taken against you by Captain First Class Branko Vuruna. It indicates in the second paragraph: "Sergeant Gusa Rajko, son of Petar, born 25 August 1956 in Gornji Zemunik." In the third paragraph, it talks about you being intoxicated by alcohol on the night of 31 May 1992 and the following day, 1 June 1992, "to such an extent that he had no control over his actions or behaviour," and it goes on it on. Now, you've already mentioned that you had been arrested at one point and detained. Was it, in fact, the case that you had been arrested because you had been intoxicated on -- on duty and, in fact, had received a disciplinary measure as a result? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence, 1D47-0037.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D825, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D825 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusa, you indicated that you surrendered to the Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask that documents to remain on the screen if not replaced by another one because that gives us an opportunity to listen and read at the same time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, no, it's in Sanction so we can't. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy if you wish for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As long as it is on the screen, I'm fine with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, you indicate in your statement that you were -- you, in fact, surrendered to Croatian authorities in October 1995. It's correct, is it not, that you were first taken to the --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were first taken to the police station in Kistanje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: In Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall when -- while you were in Knin, that you gave or you were interviewed by police officers in the Knin police station?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D47-0001, please. Just for the Registrar, the Official Note of this witness's interview begins on the next half of this page, in the Croatian version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, this is the Official Note of that interview at the Knin police station when you appeared there. If you look at the third paragraph, it says: "He further states that he was mobilised into the army of the SAO Krajina on 28 October 1991, and that he was issued a military ... uniform and a rifle with 150 bullets at the military barracks in Benkovac, where he stayed until 4 November 1991. They were transferred from the barracks to Tinj. The persons concerned states that he was an infantry soldier." Now, do you recall telling that to the police officers in Knin where you were taken --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Can I have a glass of water?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher will assist with the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is it what you told the Croatian officers there about the fact that you were mobilised into the army of the SAO Krajina on 28 October 1991 correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go on, it says that: "Upon their arrival in Tinj, they were assigned into the guard service. The commander of the infantry unit was the Reserve Captain Lalic from Polace, and the unit was composed of 40 soldiers." Do you recall being under the command of Captain Lalic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Later on down, it says: "The person concerned states that he was at the guard post in Tinj until 22 March 1992, then they were relieved. So he went to Sem Gornji where he remained until 13 April 1992. Then he was transferred to Crno where he occupied a guard post at Musaptan until 17 June 1992. His commander was Vodicarski Ljupko, an active JNA officer, major by rank ..." Do you recall telling that to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is all of the information that I just read out true?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next sentence says: "The person concerned states that Zadar was fired at from tanks, 54, guns. When asked from which direction Zadar was fired at, the person concerned states that tanks, 54, guns, and 60-millimetre mortars were deployed at Musaptan near the water supply system, and the bunker and the Howitzers and 120-millimetre mortar were deployed in Jagodnja from where they fired at Biograd and its general area." Is that information that you provided to the Croatian police true?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You then go on in this statement to say that you were then demobilised on 17 June 1992 and that you were engaged in the farming business, but that you were remobilised in December 1992 "and went to the field in Vocnjak Zemunik Gornji where he occupied a guard post i.e., secured the road through Vocnjak, PK Zadar, Vlacine PK Zadar, leading to Smokovic." Is that information true?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It then says: "The bus line Smokovic-Benkovac went over this route. He remained there until 22 January 1993, from where he went to Bare, in Zemunik Gornji, where he provided guard service all until Operation Storm." Is that information true?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I was in Vocnjak securing the road, and when I returned to Bare, my house was 300 metres away. I was in the village and the position was 8000 metres away where the army was. And I was in the village, I was not on the front line, and everything what was said before this was correct. I was posted at the village, and Vocnjak is about 500 metres away from the positions in Bare. I was in the village in the rear, some 500 metres, and the front line was below me in Goles, that's the name of the village, facing the positions of the Croatian army whose positions were 800 metres from the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But it's true that you were in Bare in Zemunik Gornji and providing guard service all until Operation Storm, correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I was there, but I wasn't there in Bare. I was in the village, exactly in the village where my house was, 500 metres behind. I was around my house, of course. We were keeping guard throughout the night, and I was there and in some elderly people. Everybody was there, it was all normal, we were guarding ourselves and others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next paragraph, it says that: Retired JNA major, Djuro Maricic, from Zemunik Gornji provided and distributed weapons to the local population of Zemunik Gornji." Now, that is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us in a little more detail how and when Djuro Maricic distributed weapons to the local population of Zemunik Gornji?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in early October when he distributed it. That's what I think. I don't know the exact date. I think it was on the 1st or the 2nd, before the real fierce war started. But not everyone received weapons. He gave weapons only to certain individuals. Only later we had so many weapons we could spare them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were these weapons given to just the villagers?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, in every, hamlet, but not to everyone because there wasn't enough weapons, initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now it says -- it goes on to state: "He further states that the firmest fortifications were set up near the houses of Zupanovi, Milkovic and at Viduka where guns were deployed. Machine-guns, M-84, were deployed in the fortification at Bare. The main machine-gunner was Gusa, Gajo, son of late Nikola, born in 1965." Now, is all that information true.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And when you say that these fortifications were set up near the houses of Zupanovi and Milkovic, what type of houses are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Those were houses which were, for most part, demolished or burnt. That's what the Serbian army did. As soon as the Croats had left, they demolished and burnt all their houses, including the church. That's what the Serbian army did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, were there fortification, in fact, set up in and around private houses in the villages?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, that was around the houses in the village, yes, because the houses were somewhat within the forests. That's where they were located, and that's where the fortifications were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say that: "He further states that the tanks, M-54, were positioned around the houses Milkovic and by the school building in Zemunik Gornji." Is that statement true?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit more about these tanks, M-54, being positioned around the houses Milkovic. Where are those houses Milkovic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: When you walk to Skabrnja, this is where the border-line is, and up to that line, there were Serbian houses. As was -- in Milkovici and Brkovici is where the Croatian houses were. Of course, the tanks were positioned near Milkovici and near the school. This is where the tanks were. They sometimes travelled through the village. One could see them. The Croats could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can just clarify, I'm advised that there is one issue I need to clarify in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And there were tanks around the school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what I said, around the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: The houses in Milkovici and the school are about one kilometre apart along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the last paragraph, please, on this page, it says: "The person concerned states that he discarded his automatic rifle at the position, as well as the uniform; and that in a tandem, he arrived in Benkovac where he couldn't find his family, then he spent the night in Bukovic." Is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Were you looking for your family in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It then goes on to say: "When he woke up, the HV had already entered Benkovac. He escaped with Slavko Rnjak into the forest, where he has been hiding until this day." How did you find out that the HV had entered Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Am I supposed to tell you that? I found out that by seeing them. Now when I turned around, there were around 300 metres away. Luckily, they didn't see us and we managed to escape. We hid in a vineyard, but we were not able to cross the road because there were tanks and their troops on the road. We couldn't pass there. We were waiting for night-fall. And when the moon was hidden by clouds, we slowly crossed the road, through their troops, and we went to Karine. This is where we spent the night. We walked through the woods after midnight. In the morning, we came to Bukora. We found some water there because we were thirsty, then a man arrived and we were scared of him as he was as scared of us. He was a Serb and he told us, "Don't be afraid. I'm a Serb as well." He gave us some food. There was roast lamb and ham and wine. We spent the day there; and from there on, we went --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the place that they want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I take it that you'll further verify that. Also I'm missing part of page 19, line 23. It is my recollection that the witness said something about distances. But could you please seek clarification of that answer. I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How far was the school from -- actually, can you tell us where the school was located in Gornji Zemunik which had the tanks next to it.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: The school was in the centre of the village between my house, called Guse, a hamlet; there was Draca as well; and further on Javori; then Markici, then Banci, Misele, Olowici [phoen], Banici, Trove. And down there were Racovici, Kovacevici, and there was another Gusa, which is actually my family nam. And the Croats were on side in the village of Drazici, Rogici, and Bulac. These is where they were, but these were Croatian hamlets. But at the very beginning of the war, they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you need for clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think, as a matter of fact, I think you told us about the houses in Milkovici. Could you tell us, the houses in Milkovici, yes, if you would walk from there to the school where the tanks were, could you tell us how much time it would take you to walk from these houses in Milkovici to the school where the tanks were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 15 minute, if you walk slowly on foot. It's about a kilometre-long road. That was the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify one point there, there were tanks both around the houses in Milkovici and around the school. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to go back to the last paragraph here on the screen because my question to you is: If, in fact, you were in Bukovic when you learned that the HV had arrived in Benkovac, you weren't 300 metres, then, from the Croatian army. Bukovic is not 300 metres from Benkovac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yeah. There's about two kilometres between Bukovic and Benkovac. But when I got up in the morning, in Bukovic they were 300 metres away. There was another man there, and we said, "Is this the Croatian army?" But he told us, "You needn't run away." His son-in-law was from Pakostan, he had and told him not to leave his house. He was a Croat. That if there were other people there, that he would come back and prepare lunch for his group. He said that nobody would touch anyone, and he told some younger people who happened to remain behind, if they had any weapons or uniforms, to change into civilian clothes and to throw away their weapons and to wait for them in the civilian clothes. That was how it was. This man didn't want to go; and we, Slavko and I, were waiting and we hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this document be marked, and tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D826, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D826 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusa, after you were questioned in the Knin police station, you were then taken to the Zadar police administration. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you were never taken to any detention centre for prisoners of war, correct, you were just taken to the police building?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. And we remained there three to four days. From there, we were taken to Split, to the prison. But I was beaten in Zadar. They knocked my teeth out and they beat me on the head a bit. I know who did this, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if we can first bring up 1D47-0006, please, via Sanction again, and we have a hard copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the Official Note -- sorry. You recall, then, in Zadar, you were also questioned by Croatian police investigators. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the Official Note of those interviews. It is, in the English 12, pages long. I'm not going to take you through all of it, obviously, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have hard copies for the Judges as well, because usually I can store it and browse through it, which I'm not able to do if it is in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We don't at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If it is not in the e-court by the break, Your Honour, I think will make copies during the break and then give it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution also be provided with a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I am told that the Prosecution has the electronic version of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Page 2, here, again repeats some of what you said in the Knin police administration -- I mean the Knin police station. Then in the second-to-last paragraph at the bottom -- let me check. This is it on page 2 in your version, Mr. Gusa, at the part that says: "Sometime at the beginning of December 1992 ..." In that paragraph, it says: "He was personally located at the position in Vlacine where they were actively on duty during the day while they were free during the night. Alongside him, the following inhabitants of Zemunik Gornji were in the group at this position," and then you have several names starting with Erceg Rajko. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Look at the names there. Are those, in fact, the people that you were on duty with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, sir? Let me ask it a different way. Did you serve on duty with Erceg Rajko, Maricic Mirko, Maricic Mile, Banic Mirko, Olujic Milan, Kosovic Radoje, and Vukcevic Petar?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we go further down past that, there is a paragraph that says: "They stayed at this position all until 22 January 1993 when the guard services was recalled. Rajko was then assigned to the 2nd Platoon of the 3rd Company, 2nd Battalion. When he was assigned to this battalion, it was under the command of Captain First Class Vuruna Branko who was, shortly after that, relieved by Captain Maricic Janko, who remained on that post all until the beginning of Operation Storm." Mr. Gusa, you were, in fact, a member of the 2nd Platoon of the 3rd Company, 2nd Battalion all until Operation Storm. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I was. But as I said, I was in the village. However, this list that is here -- that I can see here it is true. There is no falsehood here. All these people were here. It is all true. What place they were from, their birth dates, it is all true. I was questioned about this about four to five hours, and all this information here is correct. And that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me confirm then. On -- when Operation Storm began, your commander was Maricic Janko. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And beneath that paragraph, it says: "Alongside the two previously named, the following persons were also members of the battalion command," and then it lists three names: Subotic Marko ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: ... Erceg Zoran and Mizdalo Miroslav. Is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mizdalo Miroslav, there you say that: "He worked as a policeman in Sibenik. For some time, he had been in the command in Zemunik Gornji." Does that indicate -- you say that these persons were also in the battalion command. Does that mean that the command of the battalion was located in Zemunik Gornji?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now if we go to the bottom of page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in your version, Mr. Gusa - let me find it - it's at page 4, and it says: "At this position, they were split into two groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, it is the paragraph that begins right under the name Pucar Milorad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "At this position, they were split into two groups. Four days they were on duty, and then had four days off. They remained in this position all until the beginning of Operation Storm, when they were visited by the battalion commander, Maricic Janko, who told them to withdraw as they could. Already, on 3 August 1995, one part of the population was transported in the direction of Benkovac. These were mostly senior persons. The remaining part was transported on 4 August 1995. The children had been evacuated as early as in January 1993, and accommodated in the surrounding settlements in the depth of the territory of the former Benkovac municipality." Now, first of all, it's true, is it not, that at the beginning of Operation Storm, you were told by the battalion commander, Maricic Janko, to withdraw. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day you were told by the battalion commander to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but it was in the afternoon sometime, maybe around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, because already around 6.00, they entered our positions. They entered our village, Zemunik. At the very outset, while it was still daylight, they began to torch our houses. We could see this with our own eyes. We weren't too far from there. They called out to us. They didn't shoot, to be honest. They could have shot us all dead, but they didn't want to shoot. The were just yelling whoever had weapons should discard them, and we should all come to one point, and no one would touch us. That is what they were saying, but there was no shooting. They didn't shoot at us, but there were a lot of shells falling around us. But the infantry did not shoot. They didn't open fire. The only thing they did was they set the houses alight. We could see this. As soon as they entered the first houses, they started doing that. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the us a little bit more. Here in the statement, you say: "Already, on 3 August 1995, one part of the population was transferred in the direction of Benkovac. These were mostly senior persons."

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about this. How did these people leave?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, they were driven away: Some people on tractors, some on horse carts, on buses, on trucks. And from there, they were taken to Knin. So they were out of danger basically. But later on, most people left on foot and many were killed in the convoys, in these columns, because they shelled this Serbian convoy of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in here, you say that the transportation of one part of the population began on the 3rd of August. Do you recall the transfer starting before the actual attack by the Croatians began?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. In around my village, no, because we began leaving on the 4th. I mean leaving for good, leaving our native towns. And these people who were in Benkovac and Knin - we here in the villages. We didn't even know what was going on - but they, they were already leaving, especially from Knin. They started leaving on the 2nd already. I think they had been told to leave; whereas, we had no idea what was going on. We could have all been killed for no reason, for nothing. We could have been killed all, if only they wanted to. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want to clarify one point here. I'm not asking you when was the decision made to leave permanently. What I'm saying is, on the 3rd of August, was there a transfer of the senior population to an area behind the front line?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, around Bale, those who were left there, they were taken away. Well, there were few older people. Most of them during the war were around Benkovac and in the vicinity of Knin. They had all left their homes and were refugees. These were older men and women and small children. I had three small children. They were about 30 kilometres away from me, and I had to go on foot to see them because there was no other way of doing it. I took food for them and I carried all this on foot. This place was called Bukovici near Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I tender 1D47-0006 and ask that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D827 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will be going back to this document, Your Honour, but I'm going switch to another one and then come back to this in a few minutes. Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 4607, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, are you aware that the commander at the brigade level of the unit in which you belonged was named Mirko Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I heard of him, but, to be honest, I didn't really see this man in that area. I had heard of him, and I know he must be from Benkovac or from that area because I used to go to that area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat your answer, sir, after you said you knew him from Benkovac and that area. The interpreter didn't hear you, so if you can repeat what you said, after you had said that you know he must be from Benkovac or from that area.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I didn't see him often. I think he was a native of Benkovac or that area. But he wasn't an active officer. He was an officer in reserve. While he was serving in the army, he had been assigned a rank. This was in peacetime, but he was not a military man. He did not go to the Military Academy. I think he was just a conscript, and once he completed the service, he was assigned a rank. Some people would be assigned a rank of corporal or captain, some were reserve officers, some served in the police. That was my case. So, while we were still one country, Yugoslavia, my military duty was in the event of war. It was to be with the police. This would have been so had we remained as one country. So, once you have completed your military service, you're assigned a military -- military duty or military assignment in the event of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I will put it to you, sir, that Mr. Maricic, who you have said was your commander at your level, his commander at the level of the brigade was Mirko Uzelac, and what I'm showing you now is the report that Uzelac, Lieutenant-Colonel Uzelac, filed with the RSK Main Staff on the 25th of August, 1995, reporting on everything that happened during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in the English version of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Towards the middle of the page, for the 4th of August, it says: "At 1830, I received an order from the superordinate command to come to the KM," which I believe is "komando mesto" or command post, "of the GS," which I believe is Main Staff, "for a meeting at 2000 hours on 4 August 1995." Then a few entries below -- two entries beneath that, it says: "At 1900, we receive an instruction from the authorities, that it is necessary to do an evacuation of the civilian population. We transfer the order to the persons in charge of evacuation." Now, is it possible, sir, that when you were talking about Commander Maricic passing down information that you should withdraw, that the time was somewhere around 1900 hours on the 4th? Mr. Gusa, I don't think it's in the document in front of you. It's on the screen in front of you. My question is, sir: Is it possible that your commander, Maricic, passed the order to withdraw sometime around 1900 hours on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I would say that it was around 6.30 to 7.00. He was, indeed, in the village at that time, and he remained there until everyone withdrew. He said that there was no reason to remain there, that we should leave, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, the next entry talks about the meeting at 2000 with General Mrksic in the Main Staff in Knin, and there's a sentence that begins: "He," meaning Mrksic, "orders that the area of responsibility of the Corps ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... is reduced and the areas of responsibility of brigades are reduced, and that the general situation is borne in mind. I reacted and warned the commander that the 92nd Motorised Brigade was holding its positions firmly. There has been fighting, but there have not been any successes by the Ustashas in my area." My question is: Up in the area of Gornji Zemunik and the area of the 92nd Motorised Brigade of Benkovac, was Lieutenant-Colonel Uzelac correct when he wrote that "as of 2000 hours on the 4th of August, that the Croatian army had not had any successes in that area," as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, this is something that was known around 5.00 or so, as I said. When it got dark, they had already entered our village, the Croatian army. So I can repeat that as soon as they entered, they started setting houses on fire, and that's true until this day. That is the image. That's what they did. There were -- they destroyed everything, and it remains as it is today. So I think this will serve them well for tourist purposes, so tourists can see what they've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go down towards the bottom of that page in English, at the entry for 2300 hours: "By 2300 on 4 August, according to the reports of the subordinates, we had one person killed and four wounded. All lines are stable." Then at 2400: "Commander of the 3rd PBR, Djurica, called me to tell me that he was withdrawing to a reserve line just outside Benkovac. "I did not authorise any withdrawal until the last of the civilians was pulled out." Now, were you allowed to withdraw from Zemunik Gornji before all the civilians had been withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I could have left earlier had I wanted to. No one was stopping me, but I went to gather some -- collect some food. I thought maybe we would remain in Benkovac, that it wouldn't -- that we wouldn't just be expelled. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "At 2.15, I ordered the units to prepare for withdrawal to the reserve line, ordered for all the materials to be collected, for the technical equipment to be checked, and for the personnel to be held under strict command." If we go down to the entry at T-600: "T-600 Ustashas fire at Benkovac and the area of responsibility of the brigade. Since all the units of the 3rd PBR left for Ervenik much earlier, I order the withdrawal of the units on direction of Debelo Brdo-Bukovici Gaj, village of Bruska." Then if you go underneath the round stamp, Military Archives, Belgrade, it says: "I asked the base to go with the cistern at the rear in Bukovic, Bruska, Medvedje direction. Now, in your statement, sir, you mention that you arrived -- let me get it. In your 1997 statement at paragraph 9, you say you travelled to Bukovic: "When I arrived there at 0300 hours on 5 August, I found that my family was not there." Commander Uzelac here says that, at 2.15, he ordered the withdrawal, and beneath that he says, the withdrawal of the units was ordered on the direction Debelo Brdo-Bukovic Gaj, village of Bruska. Did you, in fact, go to Bukovic because you were told by your commanding officer to go to the withdrawal line which had been moved to Bukovic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I really can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps could I again put this question to you. Did you go to Bukovic just on your own initiative, in order to find your family there; or were you ordered to withdraw by your superior in the direction of Bukovic? Which of the two, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was of my own will. I decided to that on my own. I didn't even see anyone, nor did anyone tell me anything. I just decided this on my own. I went there, I couldn't find them. They had already been left, they had been taken to the right place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you went there not in the company of other members of your unit, or were they with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was on my own. I was independent. I went there, I met this man, Urnjak, and that's all. We spent the night there. As I repeat, as soon as we got up, we saw the Ustashas. What else were we to do? We just fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just tender that into evidence before the break and also to advise the Court that all documents are now in e-court so you can view them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D828.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will ask already Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. Gusa, we'll have a break, and we'd like to see you back in approximately half an hour. Would you please follow Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I get an indication from the parties on the time they would need for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have about no more than an hour and a half, Your Honour, probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No more than an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would say less, maybe an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will take us to 12.00. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It depends, of course, on the progress of Mr. Misetic's examination, but I would have no more than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That gives us an indication. So altogether, two hours to go. We will have a break and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to advise the Court, we just received a video that I'd like to play. We've disclosed it to the Prosecution. It is a video from the village of Zemunik Gornji taken prior to Operation Storm. It is undated at this point, but I will further to see if I can get a firm date on it. I would like to put it to the witness on some matters therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This came in, I do understand, Mr. Du-Toit, that there is no objection against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: We haven't seen it yet, but I take his word, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No sound is required by this video, Your Honour, by us, but we're disclosing it with sound to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we put the sound low so that the interpreters will not be in any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, I'd like to now is show you a video from a show a show emitted on RSK television before Operation Storm. It is from a video about the village of Zemunik Gornji. And I'd like to show you a clip, see if you recognise the village, and then ask you a few questions after we've watched about a minute of this video. The clip will start at approximately the six-minute mark and will go to approximately the seven-minute mark in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, do you recognise that -- these locations?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you see the -- where the person launched what appeared to be a rocket from a hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I'm not quite sure where this could be. I think it was in Goles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Goles is a hamlet of Zemunik Gornji?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That location where you saw the explosion at the end, was that the -- where the Croatian positions were?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What was on the other side there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I think the houses of Razici [phoen], the Croatian village, and I recognised only one soldier from Donji Zemunik. His name was Lavonja [phoen]. We used to call him Gare. I don't know his real name. We used to call him Gare. Now I can see him. He is from Donji Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the location I'm interested in. Do you know what that is right there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't know, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The location I am referring to, just for the record, is at the 6 minute 20 second mark on the video. Your Honour, I'm going to tender video 1D47-0094, just the clip; however, I think it is probably best if we MFI for now because the Prosecution may wish to show more portions of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. As to the date, I don't know whether there any information about the date and when it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will certainly look into that, Your Honour. If we have a date, I will provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The clip has been uploaded under this number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It will be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be uploaded and then the entirety of the video, you said, I think, it is probably best if we -- oh, you say the clip to be MFI'd at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D829, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it keeps that status for the time being. Could I ask one additional question to the witness in relation to this video. Witness, you said that apparently the hand-held rocket was fired in the direction of Razici. Is that he houses of Razici, is that well understood, and that Razici was a Croatian village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not Razici, rather Drazici. I'm sorry. This is -- this was a Croatian hamlet. Actually, it was a mixed place. There were people also with surname Gusa, and there were actually three or four Serbian households and they were surrounded by the Croat villages, Drazici, Rogici, Buljuci. Those were Croatian villages, and the place is called Goles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the place from where it was fired. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I ask you, the villages that you just mentioned, the Croatian villages and the mixed villages, were they in the territory controlled by the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or were they on the territory controlled by the Croatian forces at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These villages were under the control of the Serbian army, of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which then means that the rocket was fired within the territory controlled by the with RSK. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go back to D827, please. Now, if we can go to page 5, page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, this is page 4 in the version that you have. Now, this is, again, the Official Note of the interview that you gave to the Croatian police in Zadar. Here, at the top of the page, it says: "Rajko discarded his automatic rifle by the house where they had their position. He changed into other clothes and took some food, and, on a tandem, set out to Bukovic, where he expected to find his wife and children." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Where it says that you set out on a tandem for Bukovic, who were you with?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I was by myself and my dog.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, why did you change out of your uniform?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Huh?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why did you take your uniform off.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand your answer. Could you repeat, why did you take your uniform off?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: In order not to be caught. That would have made things even worse. But it depended into whom I would run. There were good people and there were evil people on both sides, and it depended on who I would be caught by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the middle of this paragraph, you see where the name "Subotic Jovo" is in all capital letters?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says you were taking a rest: "Subotic Jovo from Ervenik came across them, and he explained to them who was in the village, that the village was surrounded, and that they could not go any where. After this conversation, they decided to stay at his place, and Jovo approved it." It says: "In the day-time, they hid in the forest; and at night, they came to eat something. Jovo's father, Todor; his mother, Marta; and minor son, Damir, lived with Jovo in that house. They remained living there all until 4 October 1995, when Jovo's brother, Bozo, resident at Sibenik, reported them to the police." Now, your statement says that a friend in the police assisted you or advised you to turn yourself in. Here, in your statement to the Croatian police, you say that Jovo -- I'm sorry, that Todor and Marta's other son, Bozo, reported you to the police. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you also know that Bozo was, at that time, a member of the 113th Brigade of the Croatian army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was that. He was the whole war on their side in Sibenik. Actually, he was an active duty policeman before, and this Jovo -- no, Bozo and this Ivica were good friends. I think he was from the surrounding of Drnis, but he was extremely fair, and he acted properly. They gave us food and drink and cigarettes. They gave us clothes, everything. When they took us to Knin, they gave us the full bag of clothes; they gave us some kuna, their currency; and the cigarettes, but we were advised not to tell who had given this to us. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So, while you were staying at the home of Marta and Todor, my question is: Were you aware that they had a son who was a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: They said that their son, Bozo, was in Sibenik and that another one was in Male Losin [phoen]. They were on the Croatian side. I don't know what the other brother's name was. He somehow learned, I guess through Belgrade, that his mother and his father were left behind, including his brother Jovo and the little Damir, a 12-year-old boy. He cam after two months to visit them. When they came, I was watching all this from the forest. Maybe I was 20 metres away when they entered the house. I was hiding behind a bush. His mother was crying and they were trying to console her, and I heard their conversation. He asked about his brother Bozo, and they said he is somewhere in the forest, as well as Damir. Then he asked, "Is there anyone else with him," and he answered there were two strange men. Then the policeman wanted to know how we had come there, whether we were in uniform, or if we had weapons. She told him that we came just in shorts and T-shirts without any clothes, that they we had just a little food with us, and that we didn't have any uniforms or weapons. Then Ivica told her -- actually asked her, if she knew where we were in the forest, if she could go and find us. He told her to go and look for us and to tell us that we shouldn't be scared. This elderly woman, who was half paralysed and was walking with a stick, came to us and told us Jovica and three and four men in uniform, carrying large guns, had come to the house, but they said you are free to come. What else could I do? It was freezing cold and I said that would be the best way to do and let's see what happens. They would catch us any way sometime, and it was better if we gave ourselves up. If the forest keepers stumbled upon us, they might rob us. Jovo was afraid, Slavko actually was afraid, but I said, "I'm going. I'm brave enough." Little Damir went with me. We stood for a while in the courtyard. They were sitting under a walnut tree. I saw that these uniformed men with guns, but they told me, "There's nothing for you to be afraid of. We are not wolfs." Jovica got angry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He through his gun away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Is this how you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were really fair and correct. They said, "Don't be afraid. We are not animals. We are not killing people as you think." They brought them roast meet and beer and wine and cigarettes and gave us everything. Only after an hour, Jovo and Slavko joined us, and we sat there talking. They asked us where we came from. They wanted to know the exact details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slavko had documents with him. I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, if Mr. Misetic needs further details on how exactly the surrender took place, he will ask you. Please listen to his next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D47-0052, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a note, Mr. Gusa, internal, in the 113th Brigade, Sibenik. The first two pages are a cover letter from the commander of that brigade, reporting on, first, to the department for legal affairs of the Split Military District disciplinary measures that were taken against Bozo [Realtime transcript read in error "Jovo"] Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to avoid that we had a problem, I heard you saying "Bozo" Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Bozo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the transcript, it appears as "Jovo." That might create quite a bit of confusion. So it was "Bozo" that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it's one more page in, in the Croatian version. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now the disciplinary measure, it's the 26th of August, 1995. It says: "30-day military detention to reserve soldier Bozo Subotic, son of Todor, born 15 January, 1953, member of the reserve component of the Logistics Platoon of the 1st Infantry Battalion of the 113th Infantry Brigade of the HV, due to having breached military discipline." Statement of reasons: "On 19 August 1995, the said serviceman, during the execution of tasks in a warehouse, took a pistol from the technical clerk and refused to admit to the said crime. After having processed the said serviceman, he admitted to taking the pistol," and then discipline is imposed. Then in some of the other exhibits in this document is referred to the military police. Now, this Bozo Subotic, son of Todor, is, in fact, the Bozo Subotic that you encountered in October of that same year who turned you into the police. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I don't know if he was in detention, but I did see him. He came there, he knew that Slavko and I were there, and they sent this old woman if we wanted to give up. That's how it was. We would be safe as long as we were under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D830.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D830 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask you one additional question. This Bozo Subotic, what age he ap. Proximately was? Same as your age, older, younger? Could you. .tell me? This Bozo, was he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was my age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, now, you talk in your statement about livestock that was being taken away from the Subotic house. My first question is: Do you have any idea how that livestock got to the Subotic house in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: It was their livestock, and this must have been in the afternoon. They were grazing in Gare in Avli in the garden, and two or three men came and asked, and I was nearby. I was in the woods. I could just hear a noise. I heard these people coming. They were bringing coffee to the old woman. These were actually the looters. So they asked the old man, "Could you give us five or six of the livestock." And he said, "Sure go ahead." Then the other guy said, "No, no, no. Get them all." So they took them all away. They took the sheep away and some goats, about 140 goats, about 40 sheep, and a cow and a calf, and there was a sow. I guess they didn't want to take the sow with them, a pig. And when they started taking away the calf and the cow, the woman started yelling at them, and this other man -- there was a third man who was by the truck. He took a gun and he shot from about three metres away from this woman. He shot his pistol, and this other guy said why he was doing that. Fortunately, he didn't hit the woman, but the women -- but the bullet ricochetted and it hit the women -- a chip off the door hit the woman in the hand. Then when they left, I came closer and I saw that the woman was blooding. This old woman was bleeding and then I took this chip out of their wound, and then we left for the woods. There were these people who were looting, looting livestock and appliances, whatever they could find, also firewood, hay, manure and so on. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, I'm asking you: Do you know if Bozo Subotic brought that livestock to his parents' house, and do you know if Bozo Subotic was one of the persons who then took the livestock away?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't him. It was a different group. He wasn't even at home on that day, nor was his group there. This group of his, on the day when they came to get us, Bozo wasn't there, only on the third day when we said that we would surrender. He said, "No, you'd better hide, and we will come and get you, and we'll ask our command and see whether it made any point. Then we would take you to Sibenik or to Knin." And, really, as they promised, they returned on the second or third day. I think it was on a Saturday. They came and brought food and drink and cigarettes, and they talked with us and then they told us that they couldn't take us from there to Sibenik. They said that they had been told that they should report us to Knin, but because it was Saturday, they said they should put it off till Monday because there were all sorts of people. They said, "there weren't any officers there or people in authority, commanders. So maybe some of the men would beat you. So it probably better that we come pick up on Monday and take you there on Monday." Then they said, "Be ready around 6.00, but make sure to hide until we come back and until the woman tells you that it is us." That's how it transpired. It was really them. They came around 9.00. They cam in a truck, and on the truck, they had some 30 or 35 pigs, about 120 to 140 kilograms heavy each. So they loaded these pigs on the trucks. They asked us to help them. We helped them do that. Once they did that -- this took about two or three hours. We sat under the walnut net tree, we ate and drank and smoked cigarettes. Then they called Knin, and then some men came in two cars from Knin. Their police came to get us. They came in two vehicles, one driver in each car. I was in one vehicle and Slavko was in the other, and Bozo was -- no, no, I'm sorry. Bozo was left behind, but we were taken to Knin. And on the way, the man who was the driver of my car, he told me -- he said, "You want a cigarette? Here, you can light a cigarette."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
