utterances.text: Can I go back, Mr. Registrar, to D827, please. Now, if we can go to page 6 of the English version of this. This is page -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at the paragraph there, it says: "He did not provide many details in regard of the crimes against humanity and international law ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is the top in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and it is the three -- third paragraph in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But you do -- you are reported as having said that: "He heard that the attack had been executed by the former JNA and reservists from the surrounding villages, and that among them were also several inhabitants of Zemunik Gornji." Then you also say: "What he knows and can state with certainty is that Stevo Maricic killed Stura Bozo and Draginja and three females with the family name Brkic, and that he later confessed to having killed four other persons unknown to Rajko, who were probably from Skabrnja." Now, Stevo Maricic, was he from Zemunik Gornji?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you are aware that a lot of the villagers in Zemunik Gornji were involved in the killings and burnings and looting that took place between 1991 and 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In fact, in the next paragraph, it says: "He knows the names of the persons who were, to the most extent, involved in the looting and burning of the houses of Croat expellees, and he particularly highlighted the following persons ..." Now, if you look at, for example, the names here that you listed is Erceg Slavko. It says: "This man is the living evil. He was burning and looting in Zemunik Gornji." He was burning and looting Croat houses in Zemunik Gornji. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Erceg Ljuban, you say: "According to Rajko's knowledge, he was not mobilised, and throughout the time, he was engaged in selling stolen items." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Javor Drago: "Immediately before the beginning of the war, he hauled up a truck-type Mercedes owned by the company PK Zadar, which he later used to transport stolen items." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At the entry for Erceg Slobodan, it says: "Hauled up tractors, rotary cultivators, cars, and cattle, and sold it at very low prices. "Concerning the plundering of property of the expelled Croats, he said that a lot of property was transported to Bosnia and Serbia and even to Montenegro, where it was sold at low prices. The plunderers probably used it to provide for themselves property somewhere in Serbia in the case they had to flee Croatia." Do you recall telling that to the police in Zadar, sir?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You seem to have a lot of knowledge who of was doing the plundering in the area. Is it fair to say that, by 1995, the homes of Croats in the area that you had lived in were completely plundered?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Completely plundered, destroyed, and burnt down. Not one was left standing, and I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You understand that when some of these people who were expelled came back and couldn't find their belongings, they then turned to your neighbours, who were Serbs, and took things out of their homes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, they didn't do it in our place. But what could they take when they had already -- they had burnt it -- the houses down immediately. While they -- until they came back, they were in -- they were refugees, they were my neighbours, they were good people. And I'm sure that if they had come there, they wouldn't have torched our houses. It was some other people, and I'm one million per cent sure that these people, my neighbours, did not torch Serbian homes; although, the entire village was turned to ashes. The neighbours, they were very good people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to another topic for a moment, Mr. Gusa, do you know if Captain Dragan had a training camp in the Bukovic area?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I think this was not in Bukovic, as far as I know, but in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is Bruska in the Bukovic area?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I think they're in the same municipality, but it was some -- it was not very close to Bukovic. There were both Serbs and Croats in that village, but predominantly Croatian. But I never went to that place, not during the war or before the war. I just have a general idea where it was, because there were also people working with me who were from Bruska, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have 1D47-0047, please, page 1 in the Croatian -- sorry, page 2. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is an intelligence analysis by the Croatian intelligence services from the 9th of February, 1995. If we scroll down in the Croatian to the second paragraph, it says: "The 92nd Motorised Brigade is conducting the defence along the line Novigradsko More-Pridraga-Paljuv-Drace-Zemunik Gornji.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we go to page 4 in the Croatian version, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think we still missed the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Your Honour. It is all one page. We did just a very brief translation because we don't need the whole document. It is the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- and then the fourth page will be to the fourth page, which was relevant in this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There, it says: "Redeployment of one armoured mechanized company, ten T-55 tanks, and four BOV has been recorded from the Benkovac barracks to the area of Bukovic Gaj, and one armed mechanized platoon," et cetera, et cetera. Now, were there, in fact, armoured mechanized companies in Bukovic on the eve of Operation Storm? Sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which question? Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Were there armoured mechanized units in Bukovic on the eve of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I don't understand this, nor do I know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked that the exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we perhaps just scroll to the B/C/S version. I didn't see any sort of signing of the document and maybe if I can just have a look; otherwise, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although you can do that in e-court, Mr. Du-Toit. The original document comes a bit as a surprise, Mr. Misetic. It's indicated as being a four-page document and last page being page number 4 -- or it goes until, on the bottom, we find last page 5. It goes from 1 to 4 and then 5, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll check on that, Your Honour, during the next break, and we'll see what the situation is. I'm not sure why that is yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The first page seems to be a cover page, then we have page 1, then page 4, and then page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'll take a look at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I take it that, for the time being, we marked for identification until we have heard from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D831, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is the status it keeps for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, may I have 1D47-0088, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, this is now the approximate routes that you travelled, according to your witness statement. That yellow line --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That yellow line, does that accurately depict where you travelled and how you travelled?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The -- if you look at Benkovac there, you see the white line that goes down on the map and then goes to Kistanje, and then from Kistanje continues on to Knin. That's the main --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... main road between -- from Benkovac to Kistanje and on to Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I don't know if you'll know this, but the red line, is approximately where the area of the main -- sorry, the main battle position of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was on the 3rd of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I don't know that these were the positions along this red line. I don't know much about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, in the upper left-hand corner, do you see Zemunik Gornji?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Does that accurately depict that the line went basically right through Zemunik Gornji?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I zoom in, what does that mean, "going directly through"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But it looks as if some of the houses and buildings are just a bit to the north. It's a bit unclear, but at least it's close and that is in accordance with the testimony of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this, on this one, we've put the approximate distances from where you were. Zmistak is the location you said you were located, on to Biovicino Selo, and then on to Kistanje. I think that is consistent with what you say in your statement. So from Zmistak, where you were, to Kistanje is about 13 kilometres as the crow flies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, your testimony about what you saw in Kistanje, that was from a distance of 13 kilometres, correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it was just 13 kilometres, but, yes, it was rather far. Although, you could see things burning, especially at night. When it was dark, you could see the glow of the fires. Because we were on an elevate the position, we were watching this from a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you also talk about having seen military -- soldiers and trucks on the road from Benkovac to Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So what you were able to see is cars on that road at a distance of 13 kilometres and maybe more.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D832 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if could I now have 1D47-0092, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is Ervenik where you were located with all of its hamlets. Do you recognise the hamlets -- the names of the hamlets of Ervenik?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. Kistanje, Kolasac, Mudrino Selo, Biovicino Selo, Djevrska. These are familiar to me. I know this area. Closer here, there's Medvedje, Bruska, and so forth. It's all within this one general circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I am ask ing you about the -- you talk about houses burnt in Ervenik. I'm asking whether you can identify in all of these hamlets any -- any hamlets where houses were burnt?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: In Ervenik, the hamlet of Subotici; and then Brekici, that's another last name of a family; and in the centre of that hamlet was a school building. All this had been burned and looted. And also in Kistanje and in that area, it was totally torched, and I think to this day nothing has been done to rebuild it. Some Croats from Kosova, I think, or someplace like that, moved there and they live in this neighbourhood of Kistanje and Djevrska, whatever hadn't been burned down. As for Knin, Knin wasn't destroyed or burned. That's where Croats live now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you've identified -- now we're talking about Ervenik, sir. You have identified Subotici, and what was the other name of the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: There was also the hamlet of Travica. There were some Croats living there. As for Subotici and Brekici, these were villages in Ervenik. They were neighbouring hamlets that had suffered the greatest damage from burning, and I was in this area almost two months. That's how long I spent in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go to P66, Mr. Registrar -- well, first, could I have this marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D833.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D833 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Misetic, earlier, you said the witness had identified Subotici. I see that there are some hamlets appearing twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is because the boxes are the grids, and so Subotici actually extends out into both of those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not to say that they are separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then maybe one like Vujanici is linked. So that is a bit confusing here. But you say the area of Subotici would cover both of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And Vujanici, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to P66, Mr. Registrar, and it is page 9 of P66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, we -- this is a chart prepared by the United Nations Military Observers in October 1995. We've looked through this chart, and for Ervenik and all of its hamlets, the only hamlet that mentions any damage -- that is mentioned as having any damage is one that you have now mentioned, Subotici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the English version of this, please, on page 9. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Subotici is eight entries down. And in October 1995, the UN Military Observers recorded - and you can't see the top grid - but the last two numbers. In Subotici, there was one house that was totally destroyed and four that were partially destroyed. Is that consistent with your recollection of how much damage there was in Subotici?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: When I came, it was a little bit more than that. There was a school, there were a few shops, and these were also burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know if those were shops that were burned before Operation Storm or after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: After the Operation Storm of course, not before. This was on the Serbian side before that. But when everything fell and when we were cleansed, then they set fire to those shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You earlier mentioned about how the homes of Croats in the Gornji Zemunik area were totally destroyed. How many Croats lived in Ervenik prior to -- or in 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: In Ervenik? There were not too many Croats in Ervenik, but in the hamlet of Travica. And it is perhaps, I don't know, I would say three to four kilometres away in the direction of Kistanje and Knin, and this is where Croats lived. But in Subotici, there were Gornji Subotici and -- Gornji were called Tavani towards Mistanja [phoen]. And there were no Croats there, as far as I know. Well, definitely there were no Croats. But there were Croats in another hamlet, but fewer than the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, may I ask you, the grid reference which is given here, is that in any way corresponding with the squares, because I find one grid reference here for Subotici; whereas, I found two squares on your map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That is, as I -- I'll check it to make sure, but it is my understanding that that is one of the grid squares, and there's another grid because it bigger than the one kilometre by one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And does that other grid reference appear in this list somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it could be that the reporting was on one of the squares; whereas, the village or the hamlet might have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I now have 1D47-0071, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now from the police administration Zadar. It talks about the fact that you have been received on -- and this report is dated 10 October 1995. It says that you were detained because "there is a police arrest warrant issued for the same by the Zadar-Knin police administration, dated 27 October 1993, pursuant to Article 1 of the Law on Punishable Acts of subversive and terrorist activity against the state sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia." Now, when you were brought in, were you advised that there had been a warrant out for your arrest since 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: There was no warrant issued in my name in 1993. It can be checked, if necessary. They had no reason to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you understand that by acting as a guard for the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, you were committing a crime against the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't -- well, we had to guard ourselves, protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I may have 1D47 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I? I'm just trying to fully under the Subotici. Witness, do you know, in the Subotici you are talking about, how many Serb families were living in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a big village, but I cannot tell exactly how many households there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know whether there was more than one Serbian household?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, of course, there was. There were several of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, it may be clear why I'm asking this question because I'm trying to read the data on the population on the left: "Destroyed houses, 1, 2, 4." I'm just trying to fully understand whether we are talking about exactly the same as the witness is talking about Subotici and what we find under Subotici on this list. Then I see that, of course, it's the population left. Could I ask you, the houses you saw being destroyed, were these, to your knowledge, Serb houses, Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many did you see being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nearly all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many were all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least 80 percent, 80 percent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But 80 per cent, would that be five houses, ten houses, 40 houses, 100 houses? How many approximately I have to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, many houses were destroyed. I saw myself at least 100 houses. I had time enough and I was wandering around and I was also trying to save myself, and that's why I was hiding in the wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are talking about 100 houses, is that Subotici or a wider area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The wider area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- including the mixed ones like the village of Travici. I also saw it being burned. This was a little bit further away, but I saw them setting it on fire, and this was where the Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we were to limit ourselves to Subotici, what would be the number of house you say you saw being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, where I was, there was not a single habitable house, and there were quite a few of them, 20, 30, in the centre itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D47-0079, please. Your Honour, I'm reading the transcript. I'm not sure whether the reference was to 147 -- you had mentioned Subotici and a reference to 147 houses destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think, as a matter of fact, I was reading column 1, column 2, column 4. I think that is where I may have said, "1, 2, 4."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just -- you see it goes so quickly. We read the lines and then you refer to something, so then I have to go to the first page to find out exactly what the columns are. I think, as a matter of fact, I would not have given any number here. But it could also be that I referred to where you said "one" and "four" because you said there was one house destroyed and you said four were damaged. I was just, as I said before, I'm trying to read the data on the population on the left, destroyed houses. So whether I then referred to 1 in the third column and 4 in the fourth column, or whether I said I'm trying to read 1, 2, 4, I'm not certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I understand now. That's where the confusion came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusa, this is taken from a newspaper article. I'm not so much interested in the newspaper article as I am in the attachment, which purports to be a list of persons discharged from criminal authorities due to the implementation of the general amnesty act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down and go to next page at -- at number 55, next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: At number 55, it appears to be you as one of the people who benefitted from the passage of the general amnesty act by the Republic of Croatia in September of 1996. Were you aware, at the time of your release in October of 1996, that you were being released pursuant to the amnesty law that had been recently passed by the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I didn't know anything until the day that I was released. I had known -- had not known anything. I was only expected to be released and not to be executed because we were registered with the United Nations. And unless you are registered by the United Nations, they can kill you at will, like an animal. Pardon my language. All things were happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After you were released, did you come to learn that you were released because of an amnesty law that had been passed?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this exhibit be marked, and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D835.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D835 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, in your 1997 statement, you say you will -- you can be contacted through the organisation Veritas.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What is your contact with the organisation Veritas? Can you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Savo Strbac, a lawyer, worked for Veritas. He has been to Australia twice. He came to visit us. As I said, he is a lawyer, and he works for Veritas. That's how I was brought to The Hague Tribunal office in Belgrade in 1997. He facilitated that, and I remained there for two days. I was questioned for two days, all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Strbac know what you could testify about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, he is conducting this whole proceedings relating to the missing people. That's his job. And when we came from Croatia when we were freed, he met us in Belgrade. He has a residence in Belgrade. I think it is on 24 Francisko Street, the fifth floor. That's in Belgrade. It's very close to the Australian embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And when you had this meeting upon your release from prison, what did you talk about with Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: We talked about all sorts of things, but mostly how I was treated in prison. That was the main topic. He asked me if I was willing to make a statement and that the UN -- actually, The Hague wanted to talk to me in Belgrade. I said, "Yes, I see no problem with that." At that time, I was with my children in Prizren in Kosova. He called me by phone at 9.00 in the evening one day, and I said, "I cannot make it tomorrow. There is no bus service." Then I said, "I can come the day after tomorrow." I got up in the morning, I went to Belgrade, and when I arrived there, I went to my sister's place 50 kilometres from Belgrade. I called Mr. Strbac to tell him that I had arrived, and he asked me if I could come on a certain date to his office. I said "yes" and I went there. I met there with him and another co-worker of his. He said, "You wait here and a driver will come shortly to take to you New Belgrade where judges from The Hague will meet you, and there will be two interpreters as well." They kept me there for two days, and they questioned me. I had a driver at my disposal, and I was booked in a hotel. We sent the whole day together. We had lunches together. The judges and the interpreters, we all had lunches together. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And before coming --

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt at this stage. Maybe just with regard to the address that was here given by the witness, at page 63, line 24, can I maybe just have -- get some time instructions on that? Maybe we may need to redact that, but I just need to get in contact with the relevant person. I cannot make the decision on the spot now, please. I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That apparently is -- let me just have a look. The address you mentioned in Belgrade, is that an office address or is it the place where someone lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Veritas address. Their office is in Belgrade, it's a large building, and these offices are on the fifth floor. I think this is some kind of government institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: That solves the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this is the Veritas premises, then I think there is no need to follow your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: I agree. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you met with Mr. Strbac before coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When was the last time you spoke to Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: About a year ago when he came to Australia. We were in what they called the Serbian club because every nation there have their own club, and that's where we met. I think he stayed for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: We had contacts, and we got together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in these contacts in Australia a year ago, what would you talk about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, nothing political and these things. Just ask me how I was and stuff. We didn't talk about this particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you must have talked about the fact that you might be testifying in this case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: He did ask me, for example, "Would you like to testify if you are asked to go to The Hague?" And I said, "Why not?" That was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in the course after that conversation, he talked about how the Prosecution needed some witnesses to testify about shelling. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Strbac said he need some witnesses to talk about shelling of civilian areas. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, Strbac wanted to have as many witnesses as possible; and just like the people from The Hague, he came to see me in Belgrade. That's what he wanted, especially as to who had been in prison. He telephoned anyone he knew. We talked together, we spoke on the phone --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question is specifically: You had a conversation with him where he told you that it was important to testify about shelling of civilian areas, so that he could prove that the Serbs had been ethnically cleansed, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's five things in one, Mr. Misetic. I am aware of the usual practice in cross-examination. I'd like to check. When you talked to Mr. Strbac, did he say, "I want you to testify about shelling, or about being ill-treated in prison, or whether you had been a soldier"? Did he identify what he thought you could testify about in The Hague, any specific issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he wanted me to tell the truth about the shelling and my experience from the prison, and to tell how things really happened. That applied to both sides, the Serbian and the Croatian side: "You should say what you know about; and what you don't know about, you should keep quiet about."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he say that he also wanted you to testify about you having been in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He never said that, not that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he specifically mention shelling as one of the subjects on which you could testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did he say just shelling or did he say more shelling of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he said the shelling, the burning, things like that, and the people who died. Unfortunately, many were killed. Thirty-two of my neighbours were killed, and as many were wounded and are disabled now, and 32 of them dead, all of them young people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when he talked to you about shelling, did he specifically talk about shelling of houses where people would live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any subject on which he said you should not testify about this or that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, nothing of the sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic -- Yes, is there anything further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing he said to me, "Tell the truth what of saw happened; and what you know nothing about, don't mention it." That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did he also tell you that you shouldn't talk about your military service?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Some of the things you mentioned today, such as what happened in Kistanje afterwards, that it hadn't been rebuilt, et cetera, is that information that you got from Mr. Strbac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No. This is information I heard from people who went to visit the place where they were born, and these are the people who live in Australia now, and that's how I know. They saw it with their own eyes. The Croats are now living in the houses that were liveable, and the rest were demolished and burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My last question is: Was Mr. Strbac in Australia in order to assist in fund-raising for Captain Dragan's defence?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know about that. All I know is that money had been raised for defence by Captain Dragan. I was also asked to contribute, especially we, the Serbs, were asked to make a donation for Captain Dragan's defences. It is true that money was raised there, but I myself didn't give a single cent because I couldn't afford that. First, my wife died, then I spent 25.000 dollars for the funeral. And even if I had, I wouldn't give money. Anyone who is guilty should be held responsible. This is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Misetic. We will first take a break. May I take it that we can conclude with the witness today, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I probably will have not more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will conclude today. We will have a break and we will resume a bit later than usual. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic, and Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gusa.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were born and you spent, in fact, your entire life, until you emigrated to Australia, in Zemunik Gornji. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what major military installation was in the vicinity of your village? I mean the airstrip Zemunik.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: There wasn't a lot of army, a lot of military there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the military and the air base Zemunik, how far was it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, the airport was about six kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, before the events of 1995, this airstrip was held by the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: They held it until 1992, the Serbian army, until January 22nd, 1993; and then it was taken over by the -- by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And in its vicinity was the separation line, correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, you mentioned, during your testimony, that the family name "Gusa" was rather common in this area. Could you tell us what hamlet was -- what was the name of the hamlet where the Gusa family lived?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, we were the Gusa hamlet, and then about 100 metres away was Goles hamlet. Then next to them were Croats. Now the Croats were named Dragic, Rogic, and Buljot. They were good people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You know most of the extended Gusa family, right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. We met every day. We used the same bus to get to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know Radojka Gusa who was born in 1952?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. She is from Tinj, from Tinski Lisani [phoen]. She ws married to a cousin of mine, also a Gusa. This was a couple of hundred metres from my home. That's where their house was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that she was an active member of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I can lay down my life, I can bet on it that it's not true. She had three children. Her husband died, not during the war but before the war, in a car accident. She was in the car with him, but she did -- she was not killed. She did not have a uniform, and she had nothing to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And her son, Sinisa Gusa?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: He is mentally ill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, once a question has been put to you, could you just make a little pause before answering it. And, Mr. Mikulicic, if the witness would forget, you might compensate for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gusa, tell us, please, did you socialise, did you meet Radojka Gusa occasionally?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before 1991, how many Croatian families lived in your village, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: You mean in my village?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, in your village and in the general area.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: In Gornji Zemunik, there -- about 30 per cent of the inhabitants were Croat and 70 per cent were Serbs. As for the area on the border with Skabrnja, those hamlets were mostly inhabited by Croats. They were all Croats. Skabrnja was in the Zadar municipality, and the majority of the population there was Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you know Jela Prendza, a Croat woman from your village?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Jela Prendza, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in March, approximately in March of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- you went to her house, together with Radojka Gusa and Mile Graca, and told her to move out?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, not me, nor Radojka. That is not true. And if they can prove it, let them prove it; but I bet on my life, I vouch with my life, that that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. You had another neighbour by the name of Ante Stura. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This was a man who hit you with a can, a jerrycan, and knocked out your teeth while you were in Zadar in the prison?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why did he do that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Because I was a Serb. Simply put, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he move out of Zemunik together with -- as well as Ms. Preca [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: He was from Zemunik, from the same place where I was from. We grew up together, and we used the same bus to go to work in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who forced him out of Zemunik?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I don't know that. When they captured -- this was during the JNA. They were the ones who captured this village. They called them Istok. They took up -- they captured the Prenca, Vlastovici, Zemunik, Stura, Sestani, Viskovici, Bakarici, Zupane, and Skabrnja. All these were inhabited by Croats. They were neighbouring villages, neighbouring to Gornji Zemunik. In Gornji Zemunik, there were both Serbs and Croats. It was a rather large village, a big village, about nine kilometres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And all these Croats had to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and all their houses were destroyed, practically all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the time that you are in hiding in the woods, those two months. Tell us, while you were hiding in the woods, did you meet any other people who were also hiding in the woods?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I was with this man Slavko Rnjak. Unfortunately, he died in Belgrade; and there was also Jovo Subotic and his 12-year-old son, as well; as his grandparents, an old man and woman. They were 74 and 71 years old, and they lived there. They were there. Also those Croats who looted that cattle and stuff, well, we would come and eat at their house, and then we would go back to the woods so sleep there. We didn't sleep in the house because we would be discovered and then they would kill us. That's basically it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who did you get clothes from?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, when we needed clothes, we would go to the houses, our houses that had been deserted, and then I would take whatever I could find and put it on. That's how we lived then. There was a lot of clothes left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, then I would change in those other clothes because there was an abundance of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After you surrendered, you were in the Split prison, and then you were pardoned and released and you left for Belgrade where you were met by Savo Strbac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From Belgrade, you moved to Prizren, in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: True. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who sent you to Prizren in Kosova?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, the people from Belgrade, because I had three children there, three little children, and my late wife. Unfortunately, she died last January. These people from Belgrade, they moved us to Kosova, and we lived there until we left for Australia. They didn't know of my whereabouts for eight months because they had been told that I been killed at the very outset in the village. Only eight months later they learned from the UN -- or through the UN that I was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You and your family, you stayed in Kosova, but this was organised by someone, right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who organised this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that, but we stayed in a large home where it was a dormitory for students before the war. And when all this happened, in half of the building, they still housed students in the dormitories, where the other half of the building was inhabited by us, refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were there any other people from Krajina, from your area, who were brought to Kosova through this organisation?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of us in several different areas in Kosova. I reckoned there were about 1.500 of us in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After a while, you moved out to Australia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. And now I go back to Belgrade every now and then, to the Australian embassy, because I need to get medical checkups and so on. Fortunately, I went to Australia quite soon after that, and I was lucky. But seven days after I had been released from hospital, I could have gone to the United States, but I refused that. So then I was taken in by Australia. I went there with my wife and three children. But in Australia, I had three new children, twins and a little baby now. He is barely four. So now we have six -- I have six children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did Savo Strbac help you move to Australia?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, he didn't, to be quite honest. About 70 per cent of people from my village were given refuge in Australia. There are also some people here in Netherlands, some are in Canada, some in Italy and Germany. We're everywhere. So a very small number of refugees from my village remained in Serbia. As for the village itself, there were seven or eight people who are still there. They're all old people. My mother, too, returned to the village. Until then, she had lived in Novi Sad in Serbia because she had a sister there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, the question simply was whether Savo Strbac helped you. You've answered that question. Could you focus your answers on what is precisely asked. Mr. Mikulicic, could you put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My last question: Mr. Gusa, did anyone else help you move out to Australia?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: No, he didn't help me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean someone else other than Savo Strbac?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, I had a lot of relatives in Australia. They had gone there 30 or 40 years ago. So they were the ones who sponsored me so that I could get to Australia sooner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I take it that you said that this concluded your cross-examination. I was listening to the English channel and I also see in the transcript that you spoke your words when the translation was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But from your body language, you sat down, it's clear that were, indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What I said is: "I have no further questions." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Just a couple of things. Mr. Registrar, can we just pull up D833 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, you testified as a result of questions put by my learned friend about the villages in the area of Ervenik. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that you stayed in that area for about two months. Now, during that period --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can you maybe help us out, the area you talked about, it was in a mountain, and how accessible is that area, say, to the normal person? Can you drive there by a car, or must you use a wagon or some horses? How accessible is that area to the normal person, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, there was good access. There were asphalt roads. Everything was fine. There was excellent access as far as roads were concerned. Buses and cars travelled through because there was asphalt road everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And in what one last aspect, my learned friend also showed you two statements that you made, D826 and D827. Now, especially D827, it's a long statement that you made to the Zadar-Knin police administration on 11 October 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult. To tell you the truth, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, read to you some parts of statement that you made to the -- to the police on the 11th of October, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, in that statement, you gave a lot of information about yourself and also other sort of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: -- just listen to the question, please. And also other Serbs and also the whereabouts of other people within your community and within your Serbian community. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, at any stage, were you at any stage questioned about what you saw that was allegedly committed by any member of the Croatian army or police or anybody, as to what you made have through in this incident regarding August and later?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: They didn't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that your neighbours were very good people and that, therefore, they could not have looted or --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes. They were very honest people, and I guarantee that they did not burn anything. All of their houses had been looted and demolished, but they didn't do that to us; other Croats did that to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told that they couldn't do that upon return. Do you know whether they did return; and, if so, how would they manage --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. How could they manage --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please let me finish my question. How would they manage to return where you said all their houses were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Well, they came back and some of it was mended. They came back to their homes, and this is where I live. My mother lives there now. And when I speak to her on the phone, she's an old woman, she says that they are very helpful. They bring anything that she might need. My mother is 86 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you say they came back, you meant that they came back after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I have no further questions for you. Any need for further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you can help us, Mr. Gusa, you say that your neighbours weren't the type of people that would do that, but you also now testified for Mr. Mikulicic that one of your neighbours is, in fact, the one who knocked your two front teeth out, right? Was, in fact, there a feeling of revenge by your neighbours when they returned?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO GUSA
utterances.text: This neighbour that you mentioned came from the other side. He wasn't the one that I was talking about. He is to the east, towards Skabrnja. But I'm talking about my close neighbour, 800 metres, and these Croats were very good people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gusa, there are no further questions for you; therefore, this concludes your examination in this courtroom. I would like to thank you very much for coming a very, very long way, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have dealt with all the exhibits apart from the one which -- Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to advise the Court, we have sent over to the Prosecution the full 11-page document which does have a name at the end of it. We can -- however the Court wishes to proceed, I can upload all 11 pages in the B/C/S, or we were thinking just keep it to the relevant pages that were translated into English. But it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends whether the Prosecution finds anything in it which the Prosecution considers to be relevant in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you'll take your time. You don't have to answer immediately. I mean, when could we hear from you, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can we by Friday, Your Honour? Will that suit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, if by Friday, you also could have a further look at the full video footage, so that we know whether there is any other relevant portion which should be in evidence. We'll then hear from you. The date of the video is still unclear. I take it that you'll further explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will further explore, Your Honour. We haven't been able to find it during the last break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand. Could you report by Friday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- even if you do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Or earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Then we will adjourn, and from what I understand, there are no witnesses queueing, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: That is it, indeed, so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, I take it, we'll then adjourn until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn and resume on Monday, the 13th of October, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that was the 13th of October on Monday. That would be wonderful. I take that for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar never makes a mistake, so I must have misread.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, it is the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.28 p.m.
